html:
Portuguese Brazil was the colony that Portugal held in South America from 1500, when Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet touched the coast (see Cabral lands in Brazil), until Brazil declared independence in 1822.

Settlement was slow at first. The early trade was in brazilwood, a red dye wood that gave the land its name (see brazilwood trade). From the 1530s the crown handed out huge coastal grants, and in 1549 it founded Salvador da Bahia as the capital.

The economy moved through cycles, each tied to one export:

  • Sugar (1500s to 1600s): plantations in the northeast made Brazil the world's leading sugar producer for a time.
  • Gold and diamonds (1700s): finds in Minas Gerais set off a rush (see Brazilian gold rush), and in 1763 the capital moved to Rio de Janeiro.
  • Coffee came in 1727 (see coffee comes to Brazil) and would dominate after independence.

All of it rested on slavery. After an early period of enslaving Indigenous people, Brazil became the largest destination of the Atlantic slave trade, receiving perhaps four in every ten Africans carried across. Escaped slaves built their own settlements, the largest being Palmares.

In 1808 the Portuguese royal family fled Napoleon's armies to Rio (see Portuguese court to Brazil), making the colony the centre of the empire. When the king went home, his son Pedro stayed and declared independence in 1822, creating the Empire of Brazil.
sum: Portuguese Brazil was the colony that Portugal held in South America from 1500, when Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet touched the coast (see Cabral lands in Brazil), until Brazil declared independence in 1822.
